content.title: Why is there something rather than nothing?
content.summary: Creation depends on the self-existent God.

answer.text: God gives life and existence to creation while depending on nothing outside himself. Christian reasoning about dependence points toward this self-existent Creator, not toward one more object inside the universe. Scripture identifies the Creator more fully than a philosophical outline can.

reasoning.text: Created things receive their existence and depend on what they do not supply for themselves.
An ultimate explanation cannot simply be another being with the same unresolved dependence.
God is underived, not self-created: causing oneself would require already existing.

conclusion.text: The Christian confession is of an eternal Creator who gives existence, not a god who needs to be made.

sections.text: Aquinas's arguments from causation and dependence are useful historical contributions. We use Summa I, question 2, article 3 on that specific point, alongside Reformed exposition. This does not adopt his entire theology or settle the doctrines of salvation.

citations.locator: I, q.2, a.3: second and third ways

sections.title: A Catholic contribution, with a defined scope

sections.text: Romans teaches that creation reveals God's power and deity, leaving us accountable. The problem is not merely missing information: sinful people suppress truth. The gospel must therefore address our need for reconciliation as well as our questions.
sections.title: The Creator is known through his works

reply.text: The claim is not that everything, without exception, has a creator. God is eternal and uncreated. The question challenges the argument only if it shows that this distinction between derived and underived being fails.

limit.text: A causal argument alone does not teach the Trinity or Christ's saving work. God's general revelation is real, but we need the gospel to know the way of salvation.

prompt.text: What explains the existence of the things on which we all depend?
